speeches.speaker: Bob.
prose:
Signior beleeue me, (vpon my relation) for what I tel
you, the world shall not improue. I haue been in the Indies
(where this herbe growes) where neither my selfe, nor a dozen
Gentlemen more (of my knowledge) haue receiued the taste of
any other nutriment, in the world, for the space of one and
twentie weekes, but Tabacco onely. Therefore it cannot be but
'tis most diuine. Further, take it in the nature, in the true kinde
so, it makes an Antidote, that (had you taken the most de^dly
poysonous simple in all Florence, it should expell it, and clarifie
you, with as much ease, as I speak. And for your greene wound,
your Bals^um, and your—are all meere gull^ries, and trash
to it, especially your Trinidado: your
^
is good too: I

could say what I know of the vertue of it, for the exposing of
rewmes, raw humors, crudities, obstructions, with a thousand
of this kind; but I professe my selfe no quacke-saluer: only thus
much: by H^rcul^s I doe holde it, and will affirme it (before
any Prince in Europe) to be the most soueraigne, and pretious
herbe, that euer the earth tendred to the vse of man.

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse:
Oh this speech would haue done rare in a potheca
^ies
mouth.

speeches.speaker: Pis.
verse: I. close by Saint A^thonies: Doctor Clements.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Oh, Oh.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Where's the match I gaue thee?

speeches.speaker: Pis.
verse:
S'blood would his match, and he, and pipe, and all were
at Sancto Domingo.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
By gods dey^es: I marle what pleasure of felicitie they
haue in taking this rogish Tabacco: it's good for nothing but
to choake a man, and fill him full of smoake, and imbers: there
were foure died out of one house last weeke with taking of
it, and two more the bell went for yester-night, one of them
(they say) will ne're scape it, he voyded a bushell of ^oote yester-day,
vpward and downeward. By the stockes; and there
were no wiser men then I, I'ld haue it present death, man or
woman, that should but deale with a Tabacco pipe; why, it will
sti^le them all in the'nd as many as vse it; it's little better then
rats bane.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Oh good signior; hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: You base cullion, you.

speeches.speaker: Pis.
verse:
Sir, here's your match; come, thou must needes be talking
too.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
Nay he wil not meddle with his match I warrant you:
well it shall be a deere beating, and I liue.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Doe you prate?

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse:
Nay good signior, will you regard the humor of a
foole? away knaue.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Piso get him away.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
prose:
A horson filthy slaue, a turd, an excrement. Body of

Cesar, but that I scorne to let forth so meane a spirit, i'ld haue
stab'd him to the earth.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Mary God forbid sir.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: By this faire heauen I would haue done it.

speeches.speaker: Step.
prose:
Oh he sweares admirably: (by this faire heauen:)
Body of Cesar: I shall neuer doe it, sure (vpon my saluation)
no I haue not the right grace.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse:
Signior will you any? By this ayre the most diuine
Tabacco as euer I drunke.

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: I thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Step.
prose:
Oh this Gentleman doth it rarely too, but nothing
like the other. By this ayre, as I am a Gentleman: by Phoebus.

speeches.speaker: Mus.
verse: Master glaunce, glaunce: Signior Prospero.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse: As I haue a soule to be saued, I doe protest;

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: That you are a foole.

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: Cousin will you any Tabacco?

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse: I sir: vpon my saluation.

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: How now cousin?

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse: I protest, as I am a Gentleman, but no souldier indeede.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse:
No signior, as I remember you seru'd on a great
horse, last generall muster.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse:
I sir that's true: cousin may I sweare as I am a souldier,
by that?

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: Oh yes, that you may.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse:
Then as I am a Gentleman, and a souldier, it is diuine
Tabacco.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: But soft, where's signior Matheo? gone?

speeches.speaker: Mus.
verse: No sir, they went in here.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
prose:
Oh let's follow them: signior Matheo is gone to salute
his mistresse, sirra now thou shalt heare some of his verses, for
he neuer comes hither without some shreds of poetrie: Come
signior Stephano, Musco.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse: Musco? where? is this Musco?

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: I, but peace cousin, no words of it at any hand.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse:
Not I by this faire heauen, as I haue a soule to be saued,
by Phoebus.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse:
Oh rare! your cousins discourse is simply suted, all in
oathes.

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
prose:
I, he lacks nothing but a little light stuffe, to draw
them out withall, and he were rarely fitted to the time.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Ha, how many are there, sayest thou?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Marry sir, your brother, Signior Prosp^r^.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Tut, beside him: what strangers are there man?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
Strangers? let me see, one, two; masse I know not well
there's so many.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: How? so many?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: I, there's some fiue or sixe of them at the most.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: A swarme, a swarme,
Spight of the Deuill, how they sting my heart!
How long hast thou beene comming hither Cob?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: But a little while sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Didst thou come running?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: No sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Tut, then I am familiar with thy haste.
Ban^ to my fortunes: what meant I to marrie?
I that before was rankt in such content,
My mind attir'd in smoothe silken peace,
Being free master of mine owne free thoughts,
And now become a slaue? what, neuer sigh,
Be of good cheare m^n: for thou art a cuckold,
'Tis done, 'tis done: nay when such flowing store,
Plentie it selfe fals in my wiues lappe,

The Cor^u-copi^
will be mine I know. But Cob,
What entertainment had they? I am sure
My sister and my wife would bid them welcome, ha?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Like ynough: yet I heard not a word of welcome.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: No, their lips were seal'd with kisses, and the voice
Drown'd in a flood of ioy at their arriuall,
Had lost her motion, state and facultie.
Cob, which of them was't that first kist my wife?
(My sister I should say) my wife, alas,
I feare not her: ha? who was it sayst thou?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: By my troth sir, will you haue the truth of it?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Oh I good Cob: I pray thee.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
God's my iudge, I saw no body to be kist, vnlesse they
would haue kist the post, in the middle of the warehouse; for
there I left them all, at their Tabacco with a poxe.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: How? were they not gone in then e're thou cam'st?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Oh no sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse:
Spite of the Deuill, what do I stay here then?
Cob, follow me.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
Nay, soft and faire, I haue egges on the spit; I cannot
go yet sir: now am I for some diuers reasons hammering, hammering
reuenge: oh for three or foure gallons of vineger, to
sharpen my wits: Reuenge, vineger reuenge, russet reuenge;
nay, and hee had not lyne in my house, t'would neuer haue
greeu'd me; but being my guest, one that ile bee sworne, my
wife ha's lent him her smocke off her backe, while his owne
shirt ha beene at washing: pawnd her neckerchers for cleane
bands for him: sold almost all my platters to buy him Tabacco;
and yet to see an ingratitude wretch: strike his host; well I
hope to raise vp an host of furies for't: here comes M. Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: What's Signior Thorello gone?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse:
Hart of me, what made him l^aue vs so abruptly
How now sirra; what make you here? what wold you haue, ha?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
And't please your worship, I am a poore neighbour of
your worships.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: A neighbour of mine, knaue?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
I sir, at the signe of the water-tankerd, hard by the
greene lattice: I haue p^ide scot and lott^ there any time this
eighteene yeares.

speeches.speaker: Cl^m.
verse: What, at the greene lattice?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
No sir: to the parish: mary I haue seldome scap't scot.
free at the lattice.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: So: but what busines hath my neighbour?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
And't like your worship, I am come to craue the
peace of your worship.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse:
Of me, knaue? peace of me, knaue? did I e're hurt
thee? did I euer threaten thee? or wrong thee? ha?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
No god's my comfort, I meane your worships warrant,
for one that hath wrong'd me sir: his armes are at too much libertie,
I would faine haue them bound to a treatie of peace, and
I could by any meanes compasse it.

speeches.speaker: Loren.
verse: Why, doest thou goe in danger of thy life for him?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
prose:
No sir; but I goe in danger of my death euery hour^
by his meanes; and I die within a twelue-moneth and a day,
I may sweare, by the lawes of the land, that he kil'd me.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse:
How? how knaue? sweare he kil'd thee? what pretext?
what colour hast thou for that?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
Mary sir: both blacke and blew, colour ynough, I
warrant you I haue it here to shew your worship.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: What is he, that gaue you this sirra?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: A Gentleman in the citie sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: A Gentleman? what call you him?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Signior Bobadilla.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
Good: But wherefore did he beate you sirra? how
began the quarrel twixt you? ha: speake truly knaue, I aduise
you.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
Marry sir, because I spake against their vagrant Tabacco,
as I came by them: for nothing else.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: Ha, you speake against Tabacco? Peto, his name.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: What's your name ^?

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Oliuer C^b, sir set Oli^er Cob, sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: Tell Oli^er Cob he shall goe to the iayle.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: ^ Cob, master Doctor sayes you shall go to the iayle.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse:
Oh I beseech your worship for gods loue, deare master
Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
Nay gods pretious: and such drunken knaues as
you are come to dispute of Tabacco once; I haue done: away
with him.

speeches.speaker: Cob.
verse: Oh good master Doctor, sweete Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lore.
verse:
Sweete Oliuer, would I could doe thee any good;
master Doctor let me intreat sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Mount the my P^legon muse, and testifie,
How Saturne sitting in an Ebon cloud,
Disro^d his podex, white as iuorie,
And through the welkin thundred all aloud. theres for you sir.
prose:
Dic mihi musa virum: are you an Author sir, giue me leaue
a little, come on sir, ile make verses with you now in honor of
the Gods, and the Goddesses for what you dare extempore; and
now I beginne.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Oh he writes not in that height of stile.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: No: weele come a steppe or two lower then.
From Catadupa and the bankes of Nile,
Where onely breedes your monstrous Crocodile:
Now are^ we purposd for to fetch our stile.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Oh too farre fetcht for him still maister Doctor:

speeches.speaker: C^em.
verse: I, say you so, lets intreat a sight of his vaine then?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse:
Signior, maister Doctor desires to see a sight of your
vaine, nay you must not denie him.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Vnto the boundlesse ocean of thy bewtie,
R^nnes this poore riuer, chargd with streames of zeale,
Returning thee the tribute of my dutie:
Which here my youth, my plaints, my loue reue^le.
Good? is this your owne inuention.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse: No sir. I translated that o^t of a booke, called Delia.

speeches.speaker: C.
verse: Oh but I wold see some of your owne, some of your owne.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse:
Sir; heres the beginning of a sonnet I made to my
mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Cle^.
verse:
That that: who? to Madd^a Hesperida is she your
mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: It pleaseth him to call her so, sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse: In Sommer time when Phaebus golden rayes.
You translated this too? did you not?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: No this is inuention; he found it in a ballad.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse:
Fayth sir. I had most of the conceite of it ^ of a ballad
i^deede.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse:
Conceite, fetch me a couple of torches, sirha,
I may see the conceite: quickly? its very darke?

speeches.speaker: Giu.
verse: Call you this poetry?

speeches.speaker: Lo. iu.
verse: Poetry? nay then call blasphemie, religion;
Call Diuels, Angels; and Sinne, pietie:
Let all things be preposterously transchangd.

speeches.speaker: Le^ se.
verse: Why how now sonne? what? are you startled now?
Hath the brize prickt you? ha? go to; you see,
How abiectly your Poetry is ranckt, in generall opinion.

speeches.speaker: Le. iu.
verse: Opinion, O God let grosse opinio~ sinck & be damnd
As deepe as Barathrum,
If it may stand with your most wisht content,
I can refell opinion and approue,
The state of poe^ie, such as it is,
Blessed, aeternall, and most true deuine:
Indeede if you will locke on Po^ie,
As she appeares in many, poore and lame,
Patcht vp in remnants ^nd olde worne ragges,
Halfe starud for want of her peculi^r foode:
Sacred inuention, then I must conferme,
Both your conceite and censure of her merrite,
But view her in her glorious ornaments,
Attired in the maiestie of arte,
Set high in spirite vvith the precious taste,
Of sweete philosophie, and vvhich is most,
Crownd vvith the rich traditions of a soule,
That hates to haue her dignitie prophand,
With any relish of an earthly thought:
Oh them how proud a presence doth she beare.
Then is she like her selfe fit to be seene,
Of none but graue and consecrated eyes:
Nor is it any blemish to her fame.
That such leane. ignorant, and blasted wits,
Such brainlesse guls, should vtter their stolne wares
With such aplauses in our vulgar eares:
Or that their slubberd lines haue currant passe,
From the fat iudgements of the multitude,
But that this barren and infected age,
Should set no difference twixt these empty spirits,
And a true Poet: then which reuerend name,
Nothing can more adorne humanitie.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
I Lorenzo, but election is now gouernd altogether
by the influence of humor, which insteed of those holy flames
that should direct and light the soule to eternitie, hurles foorth
nothing bu^ smooke and congested vapours, that stifle her vp,
& berea^e her of al sight & motion. But she must haue store of
Ell^bor^, giuen her to purge these grosse obstructions: oh thats
well sayd, giue me thy torch, come lay this stuffe together. So,
giue fire? there, see, see, how our Poets glory shines brighter,
and brighter, still, still it incr^seth, oh now its at the highest,
and now it declines as fast: you may see gallants, Sic transit gloria
mundi. Well now my two Signior out sides, stand foorth,
and l^nd me your large ^, to ^ sentence, to a sentence: first
you signior shall this night to the cage, and so shall you sir,
from thence to morrow mor^ing, you signior shall be carried
to the market crosse, and be there bound: and so shall yo^ sir,
in a large motlie coate, with ^ rodde at yo^r girdle; and you in
an olde suite of sa^kcloth, ^d the ashes of your papers (saue
the ashes sirha) shall mourne all day, and at night both together
sing some ballad of repentance very pitteously, which
you shall make to the t^e of Wh^ list t^ lead^ and a souldiers life,
Sirha bil man, imbrace you this torch, and light the gentlemen
to their lodgings, and because we tender their safetie, you shall
watch them to night, you are prouided for the purpose. away
and looke to your charge with an open eye sirha.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Well I am ar^d in soule agaynst the worst of fortune.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse: Fayth so should I be, and I had slept on it.

speeches.speaker: Pe.
verse: I am armd too, but I am not like to sleepe on it.

speeches.speaker: Mus.
verse: Oh how this pleaseth me.

speeches.speaker: C^em.
verse: Now Signior Th^ello, Giulliano, Prospero, Bi^ncha.

speeches.speaker: Step.
verse: And not me sir.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
Yes and you sir: I had lost a sheepe and he h^d no^
bleated, I must haue you all friends: but first a worde wit^

you young gallant, and you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Giu.
prose:
Wel brother Prospero by this good light that shines here
I am loth to kindle fresh coles, but and you had come in my
walke within these two houres I had giuen you that you
should not haue clawne of agayne in hast, by Iesus I had done
it, I am the arrenst rogue that euer bre^thd else, but now beshrew
my hart if I beare you any malice in the earth.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
prose:
Fayth I did it but to hould vp a iest: and helpe my sister
to a husband, but brother Thor^llo, and sister, you haue a
spice of the yealous yet both of you, (in your hose I meane,)
come do not dwell vpon your anger so much, lets all be smoth
fore headed once agayne.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
He playes vpon my fore head, brother Giulliano, I pray
you tell me one thing I shall aske you: is my foreheade any
thing rougher then it was wont to be.

speeches.speaker: Giu.
verse: Rougher? your forehead is smoth enough man.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Why should he then say? be smoth foreheaded,
Vnlesse he iested at the smothnesse of it?
And that may be; for horne is very smoth;
So are my browes. by Iesu, smoth as horne?

speeches.speaker: Bia.
verse: Brother had he no haunt thether in good fayth?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: No vpon my soule.

speeches.speaker: Bia.
verse:
Nay then sweet hart: nay I pray the be not angry, good
faith ile neuer suspect thee ^ny more, nay kisse me sweet musse.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Tell me Bi^cha, do not you play the woman with me.

speeches.speaker: Bia.
verse: Whats that sweete hart.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Dissemble?

speeches.speaker: Bia.
verse: Dissemble?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse:
Nay doe not turne away: but say I fayth was it not a
match appoynted twixt this old gentleman and you?

speeches.speaker: Bia.
verse: A match.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: For this I finde where iealousie is fed,
Hornes in the mind^, are worse then on the head.
See what a droue of hornes flie in the ayre,
Wingd with my cle^sed, and my credulous breath:
Watch them suspicious eyes, watch where they fall,
See see, on heades that thinke they haue none at all.
Oh what a ple^uous world of this will come,
When ayre raynes hornes, all men besure of some.
prose:
Nay if it were not, I do not care: do not weepe I pray
thee sweete Biancha, nay so now? by Iesus I am not iealous, but
resolued I haue the faythfulst wife in Italie.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
verse:
Why thats well, come then: what say you are all agreed?
doth none^stand out.

speeches.speaker: Pr^s.
prose:
None but this gentleman: to whom in my owne person
I owe all dutie and affection: but most seriously intreate
pardon, for whatsoeuer hath past in these occurrants, that
might be contrarie to his most desired content.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: Fayth sir it is a vertue that persues,
Any ^aue rude and vncomposed spirites,
To make a fayre construction and indeede
Not to stand of, when such respectiue meanes,
Inuite a generall content in all.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
Well then I coniure you all here to put of all discontentment,
first you Signior L^renz^
your cares; you, and you,
your iealosie: you your anger, and you your wit sir: and for a
peace offering, heres one willing to be sacrifised vppon this
aulter: say d^ you approue my motion?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: We doe ile be mouth for all.

speeches.speaker: Clem.
prose:
VVhy then I wish them all ioy, and now to make our
euening happinesse more full: this night you shall be all my
guestes: where weele inioy the very spirite of mirth, and carouse
to the health of this Heroick spirite, whom to honor the
more I do inuest in my owne robes, desiring you two Giulliano,
and Pr^spero, to be his supporters, the trayne to follow, my
selfe will leade^, vsherd by my page here with this honorabl^
